paragraphs: In the spring of Jianyuan’s fifteenth year, yellow rain fell over Chang’an.

Where it struck the steps, the water was cloudy as rice broth left standing overnight. The willows beyond the palace walls had scarcely put forth their first green shoots before their branches bowed beneath the muddy dust. From the open mouths of the bronze beasts along the roof of Chengming Hall, narrow threads of yellow water dripped past their teeth. Before the hour of the Snake, hooves were already pounding through the mud of the imperial avenue. At the palace gate the guards recognized the lacquered black emergency token at the rider’s waist and hurried to clear the barriers. By the third gate one of his feet had slipped from the stirrup, but he remained bent over the saddle, holding a military dispatch box wrapped in oxhide hard against his chest.

Two reports were brought before Fu Jian. The Governor-General of Nanyang had written his in orderly characters: Jin troops at Xiangyang had crossed the Han River, burned two Qin border outposts, taken more than forty horses, and left over sixty Qin soldiers dead or wounded when the garrison pursued them to the bank. Another Jin detachment had struck south of Xinye by night and seized a small fort. The second report had been dictated by a wounded soldier and written down by a relay clerk. Its characters lurched across the page; the final line had been altered three times: not one of the seventeen men in the fort had returned. Their bodies could not be recovered.
Fu Jian read the reports for some time, then ordered a physician to attend the messenger first.
“He is alive,” the chamberlain replied. “The arrowhead is still lodged in his shoulder. He developed a fever on the road, after the cold.”
“Treat him first. I have seen the intelligence. There is no need to make him kneel and tell it all again.”

A register of spring planting still lay open on the imperial desk. Hedong was suffering drought; canals in two Guanzhong counties had long been clogged; and more than a dozen households of wounded veterans were still petitioning for the grain allotted them under the new regulations the previous year. Those shortfalls and the captured fort lay side by side upon the desk, two thin sheets of paper: one recording what the living would need next year, the other what had happened to the dead yesterday.

Fu Jian turned to the end of the military report and fixed his gaze on the characters for Xiangyang. Beside the city’s name was a dark-red bloodstain, as though someone had spilled vermilion upon the banks of the Han.

“Summon the Prince of Yangping, the Prince of Changle, and the Champion General.” He paused. “The Crown Prince as well. If Yao Chang is at his office, have the Grand Minister of Ceremonies attend and listen.”

It had been over a year since Yao Chang was removed from the Right Guard and given charge of court ritual. Bells, stone chimes, processions, sacrificial routes—he managed them all with meticulous care. Some said he had put war behind him. Others said a man who remembered every old road through Guanzhong need not ride them himself once he had changed into ceremonial robes. Fu Jian did not inquire into the rumors. He merely ordered the old grain-transport records for Nanyang brought in.

Fu Rong arrived first, mud clinging to his wooden clogs. He moved the planting register aside to make room for the supply-route map he had brought, then asked the wounded courier’s name. When told the man was still alive, the strain around his eyes eased a little. Fu Pi entered next, a half-dried light cuirass across his shoulders. Ever since the fighting at Wei Bridge, he could least endure anyone reminding him that he had never commanded a great battle in person. Murong Chui came from the drill ground with grass ash on his cuffs. One glance at the papers on the imperial desk and his eyes settled on the bends of the Han River.

Yao Chang arrived wearing the blue-green ribbon of his ceremonial office. He inclined his head slightly to Murong Chui. “The Champion General still carries grass from the horse grounds on his clothes.”
“And the incense of the ritual office,” Murong replied, “has found its way onto your sleeves.”
Neither man smiled. Fu Hong stood beside the desk holding three newly copied reports. Knowing Fu Pi’s temper, he passed him the casualty figures first.

Fu Pi read the sheet and pressed it flat on the desk. “Zhu Xu struck first. We need not wait for him to strike again. Give me a hundred thousand men, Father, and I shall encircle Xiangyang. At the very least I will bring those dead soldiers home.”
“A hundred thousand?” Fu Rong asked. “Have you asked how much millet the Nanyang granaries hold?”
“The finance offices can arrange the army’s grain.”
“The finance offices can write down a hundred thousand. The fields may not grow enough to feed them.”
Color rose in Fu Pi’s face, but he held his ground. “Are we to let them take the fort at Xinye without answer?”

“No one has proposed that.” Fu Rong drew a line north of the Han with one finger. “Recovering the fort and driving Jin troops back across the river is one matter. Besieging Xiangyang and taking Jiangling is another. Once you reach here”—he pointed to the crowded waterways east of Jiangling—“where do you propose to stop?”

Fu Pi said nothing. He remembered hearing his father describe how Qin had entered Ye, how cities had submitted at the mere prospect of its advance. The world had seemed vast to him then. Now the map on the palace wall appeared so narrowly gathered into Qin’s hands that only a single river remained between him and what lay beyond. A young commander’s ardor could hardly be held back by an inked line.
“If Zhu Xu comes to the rescue, we fight him. If Jiangling dares send aid, we fight that too.”
“And with every battle you march farther,” Fu Rong said, “until one day you arrive before Jiankang carrying an edict that orders you merely to defend the frontier.”
Yao Chang shifted slightly. “Such a feat might well deserve to be carved in stone.”
Fu Jian raised his eyes to him.
Yao lowered his head at once. “I now oversee the sacrifices, Your Majesty. Hearing of inscriptions, I began calculating how many sacrificial beasts the ritual office would need. I spoke out of turn.”
The tightness in the hall slackened. Quan Yi gave a small, involuntary snort, but Fu Jian would not let the joke pass.
“Since Lord Yao remembers the rites, does he also remember the wooden memorial for those who died at Wei Bridge?”
Yao’s hand stilled within his sleeve. “I do. I personally saw the lamps lit at the winter sacrifice last year.”
“If another hundred thousand men leave the passes, there may be more names to carve on it.”
“Those seventeen men at Nanyang will not return to life if Your Majesty declines to send an army.” Yao answered slowly. “The soldiers must know whether their court is prepared to stand up for them.”

Fu Jian did not rebuke him. He knew that such words carried more weight along a frontier than any edict. The bodies of those seventeen men remained in Jin hands; every soldier in Nanyang still able to stand wanted to cross the Han and recover them. Yet Fu Jian heard another voice as well. On his deathbed Wang Meng had exacted a promise of ten years. His words had scarcely risen above a whisper then, but each debate since had made them clearer in Fu Jian’s mind.
“Jinglüe asked me not to undertake a conquest of Jin with the full strength of the realm,” Fu Jian said. “The term of my promise is not yet over.”
Fu Pi seized upon the distinction. “I ask only to take Xiangyang, Father. I have not asked to cross the Yangtze and destroy Jin.”
“And if Jiangling sends an army to relieve Xiangyang once you have taken it?”
“We can defeat it and drive it back.”
“And if Jiangling is abandoned?”

Fu Pi moved his lips, but no answer came. For a general, nothing was harder than an order to halt when a city lay ready to fall. He could not bring himself to say so to his father and lowered his gaze.
Fu Jian turned to Murong Chui. “What say you?”

Murong moved a paperweight, exposing a narrow brown line between the Wudang Mountains on the map. It was a handsome stroke of the brush in the palace; to a horseman it meant broken cliffs, gullies, and summer water rising above a horse’s belly.

“Xiangyang can be besieged,” he said. “We can supply the north from Nanyang, close the mountain routes to the west, and send light troops east to cut off relief. But its walls are strong, and Zhu Xu knows how to defend them. We must think beyond scaling ladders. Can we establish camps on the south bank of the Han? How will the baggage return when the summer floods come? Where will the villages outside the city be moved? These things must be calculated before the attack.”
“The Champion General has lately become an expert in repairing canals too,” Yao observed.

“I knew nothing of them once.” Murong looked at him. “After a few campaigns I saw cavalrymen with no provisions boiling their saddles to eat. I saw victorious armies unable to persuade anyone along the road to open a door. I learned slowly.”
Fu Pi stared at the map. “I asked only whether we can fight.”
“We can. I cannot promise how many days it will take.”
“I say three months.”
“Three months from today, or from the day you reach the walls?”

Fu Pi flushed again. Murong did not press him. Pointing to the narrow ground north of the city, he continued, “A hundred thousand men would spend another fortnight crowding the supply road. Forty-five thousand to maintain the siege, eight thousand horse to cut the approaches, and the rest to build crossings and guard the grain route: sixty thousand in all. That is more than enough. Add to them, and the army becomes harder to move.”
Fu Jian ordered the grain registers from the various commanderies spread before them. He did not decide at once.

As the sun climbed, figures came in for grain issued from Nanyang’s old warehouses, the load capacities of the ferries on the Han, and the carts borrowed from civilians the previous year but not yet returned. By the late afternoon another document had arrived, more unwelcome than the rest. Over seventy Nanyang households had never been paid for carts requisitioned the year before. Several drivers had died of sickness on the road, and compensation grain had yet to reach their families. Fu Hong copied the names one by one into a separate register. When he reached the heading “deceased owners,” his brush hung motionless.
“Why have you stopped?” Fu Jian asked.
“They were alive last year, so the carts are entered as borrowed. Now that the men are dead, the offices call them deceased owners. No one has verified which families received payment.”

Fu Jian studied him, then instructed the secretary: “Settle the old debts first. If carts are requisitioned again, pay the market price. Issue return warrants before the march. If a cart is destroyed or a driver dies, there must be a record against which the claim can be checked.”
Fu Pi could not restrain himself. “Father, if we reckon everything this way, the campaign will cost a great deal more.”
“Reckon it in,” Fu Jian said. “If we cannot pay, reduce the number of soldiers. Grain does not grow on paper, and a driver does not acquire another life because I speak the word ‘campaign.’”

Murong raised his eyes. He remembered when Fu Jian, in the years immediately after Murong first came to Qin, loved nothing more than watching the frontier expand across a map. Now the same ruler was calculating recompense for wagon drivers beside that map. The change reassured Murong, yet troubled him as well. A sovereign who still dreamed of taking the world, and who learned to conduct war so carefully, might have greater means to prolong his wars.

Not until after the second night watch did the council settle its decree. Fu Jian dictated and Fu Hong wrote. Fu Pi would command the armies south to the Han. Murong Chui would lead eight thousand mobile horsemen to sever relief routes, guard the flanks, and respond to emergencies. Fu Rong would oversee grain transport, military registers, and the disposition of inhabitants after the city was taken, with appointed officers accompanying the army. The force was capped at sixty thousand; any increase required fresh authorization. No private seizure of civilian grain was permitted. Once across the Han, the army must not pursue Jiangling’s forces beyond Xiangyang. If the city remained untaken after a prolonged siege, the commanders were to report honestly before winter and request withdrawal, not summon reinforcements without authority.

Fu Jian read the last four lines himself and added two more injunctions: those who surrendered were not to be killed, and inhabitants were not to be forcibly relocated. If the walls fell, no unit was to pillage. The main force was to return north within two months.
Fu Pi held the edict without raising his head for some time. He had hoped for a victory worthy of remembrance. His father had written the road home into the orders before the army had even left.
“If Your Highness objects,” Fu Jian said, “ask now.”
“If an opportunity presents itself, must I still send back to Chang’an for permission?”
“Send a fast rider. In an emergency you may save lives or secure your camp. You may not lead sixty thousand men toward Jiangling merely because you have seen its gates stand open.”
Fu Pi clenched his teeth. “I obey.”

Fu Rong ordered copies sent to Central Army headquarters and the Department of State Affairs for verification against the tallies and registers. The rain outside had stopped long ago, though yellow mud still streaked the window lattice. Yao Chang stepped from the hall and looked up at a strip of sunset in the southern sky. “I fear,” he remarked quietly, “that once they enter the city no one will want to leave.”
Murong passed him without breaking stride. “I would be glad if they all lived long enough to face that choice.”

In the fifth month, sixty thousand Qin troops marched past Nanyang. Wagon ruts ran deep through the road from day into night, filling with water. Barefoot drivers pushed from behind while their boots hung from the shafts to dry. Fu Shao went south with the left camp. On his rounds after nightfall he found Liang Aguo mending a torn sleeve beside the fire; Helan Wu had dragged his saddle farther away lest sparks catch the leather. The two began quarreling over a little bag of salt, and Fu Shao, weary of the noise, shouted through the tent flap before they fell silent.

At the Yu River someone secretly stitched an old banner into his bundle, claiming that carrying it would ward off arrows. Fu Shao did not cut it to pieces. He had the flag folded and put away, and ordered that only Qin unit numbers be displayed before the enemy. That night the soldier came to ask for his banner back. Fu Shao handed it over and pointed toward the black water beyond the camp. “Keep it safe. If you go into battle tomorrow, take your orders only from the bronze gong ahead.” The man accepted the cloth and walked away with his head lowered.

Before the army crossed the Han, Murong Chui personally inspected the north-bank ferries. Camps for sixty thousand men stretched along the river. Grain carts, timber palisades, and craftsmen’s sheds had their appointed places, but the officers passing between them still argued bitterly. Which company crossed first, whose horses would founder in the mud—when tempers rose, old grievances and home dialects came spilling out together. Murong listened and ordered everyone to follow the ferry register in sequence. Anyone who cut the line would be reported along with his commanding officer. Men grumbled after the order, but not one battalion dared cross without leave.

Early in the sixth month, Qin encampments appeared north of Xiangyang. Half the fields outside the city already lay abandoned; newly cut ditches wound across the river flats. Jin signal fires gave off smoke by day and flame by night. Wearing his armor, Zhu Xu climbed the wall. Across the river he saw no familiar black banners of the Di, no white horsehair standards of the Xianbei, no oxhide camp gates keeping each people apart. The red Qin flags now marked only numbered units. He lifted his viewing tube and saw one cavalry column give way to marching infantry while the wagons behind halted in rhythm with the bronze signal gong.
“The northerners look like one army this time,” his deputy said.

Zhu Xu did not answer. He kept the tube trained on the northern bank for a long while. Qin soldiers were cutting timber and driving piles beside the river. He knew that from that night onward the water would no longer prevent them from building bridges. Behind him the gates of Xiangyang would need two more bars before dark.
“Bring me the war drums.”
“They have not attacked,” his deputy said. “Why sound the drums now?”
Zhu Xu tightened his helmet. “So the people inside the city can hear them.”

The first mallet fell. One after another, the four gates of Xiangyang answered. Bowyers repairing arrows lifted their heads; a fishwife dragged the last of her baskets back into the lane; on the wall, a newly enlisted boy gripped his spear so tightly that sweat made its wooden shaft slippery. From across the Han came the answering horns of Qin. Their voices passed back and forth through the river mist until dusk, when even the small grain boats upon the water seemed to tremble.
